notes:
Pressure

  • Pressure $P = F/A$ (Pa = N m$^{-2}$). Pressure at depth $h$ in a fluid of density $\rho$: $P = P_0 + \rho g h$.
  • Pascal's law: pressure applied at any point of an enclosed incompressible fluid is transmitted equally in all directions. Hydraulic lift: $\dfrac{F_1}{A_1} = \dfrac{F_2}{A_2}$.
  • Atmospheric pressure $= 1.013\times10^5$ Pa $=76$ cm of Hg.

Buoyancy

  • Archimedes' principle: upthrust $= $ weight of fluid displaced $= V_{sub}\rho_{fluid}\,g$.
  • A body floats when average density $\le$ fluid density; fraction submerged $= \rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid}$.

Fluid flow

QuantityRelation
Equation of continuity$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ (mass conservation, incompressible)
Bernoulli's theorem$P + \dfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$ (energy conservation along a streamline)
Torricelli / speed of efflux$v = \sqrt{2gh}$
Venturimeterspeed$\uparrow$ $\Rightarrow$ pressure$\downarrow$ (narrow section)

Viscosity

  • Newton's law: viscous force $F = \eta A \dfrac{dv}{dx}$; SI unit of $\eta$ is poiseuille (Pa s).
  • Stokes' law: viscous drag on a sphere $F = 6\pi\eta r v$.
  • Terminal velocity: $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9\eta}$ ($\rho$ = density of sphere, $\sigma$ = density of fluid). Reached when weight $=$ upthrust $+$ viscous drag.
  • Reynolds number $R_e = \rho vd/\eta$: laminar flow for $R_e < 1000$, turbulent above $\sim2000$.

Surface tension

  • $T = F/l$ (N m$^{-1}$) $=$ surface energy per unit area (J m$^{-2}$).
  • Excess pressure inside a liquid drop/bubble in air: $\Delta P = 2T/r$; inside a soap bubble (two surfaces): $\Delta P = 4T/r$.
  • Capillary rise: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$; $\theta$ = angle of contact (0° for water-glass, obtuse for mercury-glass, which is why mercury depresses in a capillary).
  • Surface tension decreases with rise in temperature and with addition of detergent/impurity (usually).

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 2 questions from this chapter, usually one numerical on viscosity/terminal velocity or Bernoulli's equation and one on surface tension/capillarity. Memorise the $2T/r$ vs $4T/r$ distinction and the terminal velocity formula — they are asked almost every year.

questions.q: The pressure at a depth of 5 m below the free surface of water (density 1000 kg m$^{-3}$) in excess of atmospheric pressure is (g = 10 m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $P = \rho gh = 1000\times10\times5 = 5\times10^4$ Pa.
questions.trick: $P=\rho gh$ — plug depth, density, $g$ directly, no atmospheric term needed.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift, the smaller piston has area 5 cm$^2$ and the larger piston has area 500 cm$^2$. A force of 50 N applied on the smaller piston supports a load of
questions.trick: Hydraulic lift: $F_2=F_1(A_2/A_1)$ — force scales with area ratio.

questions.q: A block of wood of density 600 kg m$^{-3}$ floats in water of density 1000 kg m$^{-3}$. The fraction of its volume above the water surface is
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged $= \rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid} = 0.6$, so fraction above $= 1-0.6 = 0.4$.
questions.trick: Fraction submerged $=\rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid}$; fraction above $=1-$ that.

questions.q: Water flows through a horizontal pipe of varying cross-section. At a point where the area is 4 cm$^2$, the speed is 3 m s$^{-1}$. The speed at a point where the area is 2 cm$^2$ is
questions.explanation: Equation of continuity: $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 \Rightarrow v_2 = 4\times3/2 = 6$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Continuity: $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$ — narrower area means proportionally faster flow.

questions.q: Water stored in a tank up to a height $H$ escapes through a small hole at the bottom. The speed of efflux is
questions.explanation: By Bernoulli's theorem (Torricelli's law), $v = \sqrt{2gH}$.
questions.trick: Torricelli: efflux speed $=\sqrt{2gh}$ — same as free-fall speed formula.

questions.q: According to Bernoulli's theorem, at a constriction in a horizontal pipe where the fluid speed increases, the pressure
questions.explanation: For horizontal flow $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 = $ constant; higher $v$ means lower $P$ (this is the principle used in a venturimeter and carburettor).
questions.trick: Bernoulli: speed up $\Rightarrow$ pressure down (venturi/carburettor principle).

questions.q: A metal sphere of radius $r$ falls through a viscous liquid and attains terminal velocity $v_t$. If the radius is doubled (same materials), the new terminal velocity is
questions.explanation: $v_t \propto r^2$, so doubling $r$ makes $v_t$ four times.
questions.trick: $v_t\propto r^2$ (Stokes) — double radius, quadruple terminal velocity.

questions.q: A raindrop of radius 1 mm falls through air. Given the terminal velocity depends on $2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta$, if the density of air is neglected compared to water, terminal velocity is proportional to
questions.explanation: From the Stokes' law terminal velocity formula, $v_t \propto r^2$ when all other quantities are fixed.
questions.trick: Terminal velocity formula's $r^2$ factor directly gives $v_t\propto r^2$.

questions.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $r$ and surface tension $T$ is
questions.explanation: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer film surfaces), so $\Delta P = 4T/r$, unlike a liquid drop which has only one surface ($2T/r$).
questions.trick: Soap bubble has two surfaces $\Rightarrow\Delta P=4T/r$ (drop: $2T/r$).

questions.q: Two soap bubbles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm (same liquid) coalesce under isothermal conditions to form a single bubble. The radius of the new bubble is
questions.explanation: Surface energy is conserved: $r^2 = r_1^2+r_2^2$ (since $\Delta P\cdot dV$ work argument gives $r_1^2+r_2^2=r^2$ for bubbles) $=9+16=25 \Rightarrow r=5$ cm.
questions.trick: Bubble coalescence conserves surface energy: $r^2=r_1^2+r_2^2$.

questions.q: Water rises to a height of 4 cm in a capillary tube of radius $r$. If the radius is doubled, the new height of rise is
questions.explanation: $h = \dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r} \propto \dfrac1r$; doubling $r$ halves $h$ to 2 cm.
questions.trick: $h\propto1/r$ (capillary rise) — doubling radius halves the rise.

questions.q: Mercury does not wet glass and shows a depression in a capillary tube because the angle of contact for mercury-glass is
questions.explanation: Mercury-glass has an obtuse angle of contact ($\approx 140^\circ$), which makes $\cos\theta$ negative, giving depression instead of rise.
questions.trick: Obtuse contact angle $\Rightarrow\cos\theta<0\Rightarrow$ depression, not rise.

questions.q: The surface tension of a liquid, in general, ______ as its temperature increases.
questions.explanation: Molecular attraction weakens with rising temperature, so surface tension decreases (it becomes zero at the critical temperature).
questions.trick: Heat weakens molecular attraction $\Rightarrow$ surface tension falls with temperature.

questions.q: A liquid drop of radius $R$ splits into 8 identical smaller drops. Given surface energy $=T\times$ surface area, the surface energy of the system
questions.explanation: Volume conservation: $R^3 = 8r^3 \Rightarrow r=R/2$. Total new area $=8(4\pi r^2)=8\times4\pi (R/2)^2=8\pi R^2$, which is $2\times$ the original area $4\pi R^2$, so surface energy doubles.
questions.trick: Volume fixed, area up on splitting $\Rightarrow$ smaller drops mean more surface energy.

questions.q: A fluid flowing through a tube of non-uniform cross-section obeys the equation of continuity $Av=$ constant. This follows directly from conservation of
questions.explanation: For an incompressible fluid, the mass flowing per second must be the same everywhere along the tube, giving $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$.
questions.trick: Continuity equation $Av=$const is just mass conservation for incompressible flow.

questions.q: An object weighs 20 N in air and 15 N when fully immersed in water. Its relative density is
questions.explanation: Upthrust $=20-15=5$ N $= $ weight of water displaced. Relative density $=\dfrac{\text{weight in air}}{\text{upthrust}}=\dfrac{20}{5}=4$.
questions.trick: Relative density $=$ weight in air $\div$ (weight in air $-$ weight in water).

questions.q: For flow to remain laminar (streamlined) in a pipe, the Reynolds number should be
questions.explanation: $R_e = \rho vd/\eta$; flow is laminar for $R_e$ below roughly 1000 and turbulent above about 2000, with an unstable region in between.
questions.trick: Recall cutoffs: $R_e<1000$ laminar, $R_e>2000$ turbulent, in between unstable.

questions.q: A small ball is dropped gently into a viscous liquid. It eventually moves with constant terminal velocity because at that stage
options: the net force on it is zero
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity, weight $=$ upthrust $+$ viscous drag, so the net force (and hence acceleration) is zero and velocity stays constant.
questions.trick: Terminal velocity $\Rightarrow$ constant speed $\Rightarrow$ net force $=0$ (weight $=$ upthrust $+$ drag).

questions.q: SI unit of coefficient of viscosity ($\eta$) is
questions.explanation: From $F=\eta A\,dv/dx$, $\eta = \dfrac{F\,dx}{A\,dv}$, units N m/(m$^2$·m s$^{-1}$) = N s m$^{-2}$ = Pa s (also called poiseuille).
questions.trick: $\eta$'s SI unit is poiseuille $=$ Pa s; derive from $F=\eta A\,dv/dx$.

questions.q: A venturimeter is used to measure the
options: speed of flow of a liquid
questions.explanation: A venturimeter uses the pressure difference between a wide and a narrow section (Bernoulli's principle) to determine the flow speed of a liquid.
questions.trick: Venturimeter uses pressure drop at a constriction to find flow speed.

questions.q: Pascal's law states that pressure applied at any point of an enclosed, incompressible fluid
options: is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container
decreases as it is transmitted farther from the point of application
is transmitted only in liquids, never in gases
is transmitted only along the direction in which it was applied
questions.explanation: This is the statement of Pascal's law, which is the working principle of hydraulic lifts, jacks and brakes.
questions.trick: Pascal's law: pressure transmits equally, undiminished, in every direction.

questions.q: Standard atmospheric pressure ($1.013\times10^5$ Pa) is equivalent to a mercury column of height
questions.explanation: By definition, standard atmospheric pressure supports a mercury column 76 cm high.
questions.trick: Memorise: 1 atm $=1.013\times10^5$ Pa $=76$ cm of Hg.

questions.q: Three vessels A, B and C, having very different shapes (narrow, wide, conical) but the same base area, are filled with water to the same height. The pressure exerted by the water on the base of each vessel is
options: greatest for the conical vessel C
greatest for the narrowest vessel A
the same for all three vessels, since pressure depends only on the height and density of the liquid column, not on the shape of the container
greatest for the widest vessel B
questions.explanation: $P=\rho gh$ depends only on the depth and density of the liquid, not on the shape or cross-section of the container — this is the hydrostatic paradox.
questions.trick: Hydrostatic paradox: $P=\rho gh$ ignores container shape — same base pressure everywhere.

questions.q: A tyre pressure gauge reads 200 kPa. If atmospheric pressure is 100 kPa, the absolute pressure of the air inside the tyre is
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure $=$ absolute pressure $-$ atmospheric pressure, so absolute pressure $=200+100=300$ kPa.
questions.trick: Absolute $=$ gauge $+$ atmospheric — always add the two given pressures.

questions.q: Water flows through a horizontal tube whose cross-section narrows. The speed is 1 m/s in the wide section and 4 m/s in the narrow section. Using Bernoulli's equation, the pressure difference between the wide and narrow sections (density of water $=1000$ kg m$^{-3}$) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta P = \frac12\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2) = \frac12\times1000\times(16-1)=7500$ Pa.
questions.trick: Bernoulli (horizontal): $\Delta P=\frac12\rho(v_2^2-v_1^2)$ — square the speeds, subtract, halve.

questions.q: An aircraft wing is shaped (cambered) so that air moves faster over its curved upper surface than beneath it. By Bernoulli's principle, this produces
options: increased drag but no vertical force
a net upward force (lift), because the faster-moving air above the wing is at lower pressure than the slower air below
a downward force pulling the aircraft toward the ground
no net force, since both surfaces experience identical pressure
questions.explanation: Faster flow over the top means lower pressure there (Bernoulli's theorem); the resulting pressure difference produces the net upward lift force.
questions.trick: Faster air on top (Bernoulli) $\Rightarrow$ lower pressure there $\Rightarrow$ net lift up.

questions.q: For streamline flow of a liquid through a narrow horizontal tube under a fixed pressure difference (Poiseuille's law, rate $\propto r^4$), if the tube's radius is doubled, keeping all else constant, the volume flow rate becomes
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's equation gives volume flow rate $\propto r^4$; doubling $r$ increases the rate by $2^4=16$ times.
questions.trick: Poiseuille: rate $\propto r^4$ — doubling radius gives $2^4=16\times$ flow.

questions.q: A small sphere of radius 1 mm falls through a viscous liquid and attains a terminal velocity of 0.02 m s$^{-1}$. If the density difference between the sphere and the liquid is 9000 kg m$^{-3}$ ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$), the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is
questions.explanation: $\eta = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g}{9v_t} = \dfrac{2\times(10^{-3})^2\times9000\times10}{9\times0.02} = \dfrac{0.18}{0.18}=1$ Pa s.
questions.trick: Terminal velocity: $\eta=2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/(9v_t)$ — direct plug-in, watch mm$\to$m.

questions.q: When several small liquid drops coalesce into one large drop, the total surface area decreases. The corresponding decrease in surface energy usually appears as
options: an increase in the liquid's surface tension
kinetic energy of the drop moving away
heat, causing a small rise in the temperature of the liquid
an increase in the liquid's mass
questions.explanation: Surface energy released when the area decreases on coalescence is converted mainly into heat, slightly warming the resulting drop.
questions.trick: Coalescence: lost surface energy $\to$ heat, slightly warms the merged drop.

questions.q: Adding detergent to water lowers its surface tension. As a result, the height to which the soapy water rises in a fine capillary tube, compared to pure water, is
options: infinite, since soap solutions do not obey the capillary rise formula
questions.explanation: $h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$; a lower surface tension $T$ directly gives a smaller rise $h$.
questions.trick: $h\propto T$ directly (capillary rise) — lower $T$ from detergent means smaller $h$.

questions.q: For water (density 1000 kg m$^{-3}$, viscosity $1\times10^{-3}$ Pa s) flowing through a pipe of diameter 2 cm, using $R_e=\rho vd/\eta$, the flow becomes turbulent ($R_e>2000$) once the speed exceeds approximately
questions.explanation: $v = \dfrac{R_e\,\eta}{\rho d} = \dfrac{2000\times10^{-3}}{1000\times0.02} = \dfrac{2}{20}=0.1$ m/s.
questions.trick: Set $R_e=2000$, solve $v=R_e\eta/(\rho d)$ for the turbulence threshold speed.

questions.q: As temperature increases, the viscosity of a liquid generally _____, while the viscosity of a gas generally _____.
questions.explanation: In liquids, weaker intermolecular cohesion at higher temperature lowers viscosity; in gases, viscosity arises from molecular momentum transfer, which increases with temperature, so gas viscosity rises.
questions.trick: Liquids: viscosity falls with heat (weaker cohesion); gases: rises (more molecular collisions).

questions.q: In a U-tube, a column of oil 10 cm high balances a column of water 8 cm high, measured from the common interface. The density of the oil is (density of water $=1000$ kg m$^{-3}$)
questions.explanation: At the common interface, pressures balance: $\rho_{oil}gh_{oil}=\rho_{water}gh_{water}$, so $\rho_{oil}=1000\times8/10=800$ kg m$^{-3}$.
questions.trick: U-tube balance: $\rho_1h_1=\rho_2h_2$ at the common interface — cross-multiply.

questions.q: Water escapes horizontally through a small hole at depth $h$ below the free surface of a tank filled to a total height $H$. The horizontal range of the jet on the ground is maximum when
questions.explanation: Range $=2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$, which is maximised at $h=H/2$, giving the maximum range equal to $H$.
questions.trick: Efflux range $=2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$ is maximised at $h=H/2$ (like projectile symmetry).

questions.q: A spinning ball moving through air often follows a curved path (as used, for example, in swing bowling in cricket). This is because
options: the ball's spin makes air move faster on one side and slower on the other, creating a pressure difference (Magnus effect) by Bernoulli's principle
air resistance is zero on one side of a spinning ball
spinning objects lose mass unevenly, curving their path
gravity acts unevenly on a spinning object
questions.explanation: The relative air speeds on the two sides of the spinning ball differ, so by Bernoulli's principle the pressures differ, producing a net sideways (Magnus) force that curves the path.
questions.trick: Spin makes air speeds unequal on two sides $\Rightarrow$ Bernoulli pressure gap $\Rightarrow$ Magnus curve.

questions.q: In Poiseuille's equation for streamline flow, if the pressure difference across a tube is doubled and its length is also doubled (radius and viscosity unchanged), the volume flow rate becomes
questions.explanation: Rate $\propto P/L$; doubling both $P$ and $L$ leaves the ratio $P/L$, and hence the flow rate, unchanged.
questions.trick: Poiseuille rate $\propto P/L$ — doubling both leaves the ratio, hence rate, unchanged.

questions.q: Water rises to a height of 3 cm in a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm ($\rho=1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, angle of contact $\approx0°$). The surface tension of water is approximately
questions.explanation: $T=\dfrac{h\rho g r}{2\cos\theta}=\dfrac{0.03\times1000\times10\times0.0005}{2}=0.075$ N/m.
questions.trick: $T=h\rho gr/(2\cos\theta)$ — rearranged capillary-rise formula, plug and simplify.

questions.q: An iceberg of density 900 kg m$^{-3}$ floats in seawater of density 1030 kg m$^{-3}$. The fraction of the iceberg's volume that remains above the water surface is approximately
questions.explanation: Fraction submerged $=\rho_{ice}/\rho_{sea}=900/1030\approx0.874$; fraction above the surface $\approx1-0.874=0.126=12.6\%$.
questions.trick: Fraction above $=1-\rho_{ice}/\rho_{sea}$ — compute the density ratio first.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT work on the principle of Pascal's law?
options: a venturimeter (which instead relies on Bernoulli's principle)
questions.explanation: Hydraulic lifts, brakes and jacks all transmit an applied pressure through an enclosed fluid (Pascal's law); a venturimeter instead measures flow speed using the pressure drop predicted by Bernoulli's theorem.
questions.trick: Pascal's law devices transmit pressure (lift, brake, jack); venturimeter is Bernoulli-based.

questions.q: Two soap bubbles of different radii, formed at the two ends of a tube with a stopcock, are connected by opening the stopcock. Air flows from the smaller bubble into the larger one until the smaller one collapses. This happens because
options: the smaller bubble has a higher excess internal pressure ($\Delta P = 4T/r$, inversely proportional to $r$), so air flows from it to the lower-pressure larger bubble
surface tension always favours the larger bubble growing at the expense of any smaller one, regardless of pressure
the larger bubble has a lower surface tension
the smaller bubble has a lower internal pressure and forces air out
questions.explanation: Since $\Delta P=4T/r$, a smaller radius gives a larger excess pressure; air therefore flows from the high-pressure smaller bubble into the larger, lower-pressure one until the smaller bubble empties and collapses.
questions.trick: Smaller bubble has higher $\Delta P=4T/r$ $\Rightarrow$ air flows small $\to$ large.
